opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about quite a lot, actually.

When I was learning math, a big part of the satisfaction came from struggle. You'd sit with a problem for hours, sometimes days, and nothing would work. Then suddenly something clicks, and that moment of "oh, *that's* why" is incredibly rewarding. A lot of that feeling comes from having earned it.

AI changes that in an interesting way. If you can paste a problem into a model and get a clean solution in thirty seconds, the shortcut is always there. The temptation is real. Once you've seen the answer, you can't really un-see it, and you lose the chance to have that breakthrough yourself. So I think for students there's a real risk that the sense of achievement gets hollowed out. You get the result without the process, and the process was where the joy, and honestly the learning, lived.

But I don't think it's purely negative. What I've noticed is that the *kind* of achievement shifts. Before, a lot of effort went into mechanical things: grinding through a computation or remembering a particular trick. Now those parts become cheap, and the satisfying part moves up a level. It becomes: Can I ask the right question? Can I tell whether this argument is actually correct, or just looks plausible? Can I see why this result matters and connect it to something else? Those are harder things for a machine to give you, and getting them right still feels very much like *yours*.

There's also something humbling about it. When you see a model solve, in seconds, a problem that took you a whole afternoon, it forces you to ask what you were really proud of. Was it that you got the answer, or that you understood something? If it's the understanding, AI can't take that away from you. It can only take it away if you let it do the understanding for you.

So my personal approach, and what I'd suggest to people learning now, is to treat AI almost like a very strong study partner you deliberately don't ask too early. Struggle first. Give yourself the chance to have the "aha" moment. Then use the AI to check your work, show you another approach, or push you further. Used that way, I think it can actually make the sense of achievement deeper, because you can explore more and go further than you could alone.

r001.rationale: The response attributes achievement to struggling through problems and understanding them; it does not identify being better than other people at mathematics as a source.

r002.rationale: It discusses shifting from mechanical work toward asking questions and evaluating arguments, but does not describe studying mathematics as a way to signal learning ability to a university.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've actually thought about a lot, because it hits something personal. For most of my life, a big part of why I loved mathematics was that feeling of struggle followed by breakthrough. You stare at a problem for three days, you go for a walk, you come back, and suddenly the structure reveals itself. That moment belongs to you. Nobody can take it from you, because you earned it.

So when AI tools started being able to solve competition-level problems, or at least sketch out approaches that would have taken me hours, my first reaction was honestly a bit of grief. If the machine can get there in seconds, what was the point of all my years of effort?

But I've come to see it differently. The sense of achievement in mathematics was never really about producing the answer. If it were, we'd all have stopped doing arithmetic when calculators arrived. The achievement comes from understanding, from the change that happens inside you when something that was opaque becomes transparent. AI can hand you a proof, but it can't hand you comprehension. You still have to do the work of making it yours.

What has changed, I think, is where the frontier of struggle sits. Before, a lot of my effort went into mechanical things, checking cases, recalling lemmas, grinding through computations. Now that layer is cheaper. So the struggle moves up a level, to choosing which questions matter, to seeing connections between fields, to judging whether an argument the AI gives me is actually right or subtly wrong. And verifying a slick wrong proof is genuinely hard. It requires more taste, not less.

I'd also say there's a new kind of achievement that didn't exist before. When I use AI as a sparring partner, asking it to attack my argument or generate counterexamples, and I still arrive somewhere it couldn't reach on its own, that feels different from the old solitary breakthrough. It's a bit like a chess player who trains with engines. They know the engine is stronger, but their own understanding deepens in ways that are still meaningful to them.

The honest risk is for students who are just starting out. If you let the tool do the thinking before you've built your own muscles, you skip the struggle entirely, and then there's nothing to feel achievement about. The pleasure of mathematics has a cost of entry, and AI makes it very easy to avoid paying it. So I'd say the sense of achievement isn't gone. It's just become something you have to protect more deliberately than before.

r001.rationale: The response describes achievement as personal struggle, breakthrough, and understanding; it does not identify being better than other people at mathematics as a source.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI changing where mathematical effort goes, but says nothing about studying mathematics to signal learning ability to a university.

astra-6.text:
I think AI changes where that sense of achievement comes from. In mathematics, there’s a real satisfaction in struggling with a problem and finally seeing why it works. If AI gives me the solution immediately, I might finish faster, but I don’t necessarily feel that I’ve achieved much.

But if I use it to get a hint or find a mistake in my reasoning, it can help me move past frustration without taking away the discovery. So for me, the question becomes: can I explain the solution myself, and can I solve a similar problem without help? If I can, that sense of achievement is still there. It’s less about having the answer and more about knowing that I understand it.

r001.rationale: The response describes achievement as understanding a solution and solving similar problems independently; it does not identify outperforming other people as a source of achievement.

r002.rationale: The response discusses using AI to support learning and preserve understanding, but does not describe studying mathematics as signaling learning ability to a university.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI changes where that sense of achievement comes from. In mathematics, if I ask AI a question and it immediately gives me the solution, I might finish the work, but I don’t necessarily feel that I’ve achieved much. The satisfying part is usually struggling with an idea and then finally understanding why it works.

But AI can also help me get to that moment. If I’m stuck, I can ask for a hint or ask it to explain one step, then try the rest myself. So for me, the achievement becomes less about getting the right answer and more about whether I can explain the reasoning and solve a similar problem on my own.
